introduction.text: The Column of Marcus Aurelius is a Roman victory column in Piazza Colonna, Rome, built to honor Emperor Marcus Aurelius and his campaigns against Germanic tribes. It is a key monument that links Roman imperial propaganda, architectural tradition, and the history of the Marcomannic Wars.

history.description: The column commemorates the Marcomannic Wars fought by Marcus Aurelius from 169 to 180 AD.
Construction began after Marcus Aurelius' death in 180 AD and was completed around 193 AD under Septimius Severus.
The bronze statue atop the column was originally of Marcus Aurelius and was replaced by St. Paul in the 16th century.
In 1589 Pope Sixtus V commissioned a restoration that replaced the missing bronze statue of Marcus Aurelius with one of St. Paul.
The column was modeled after Trajan's Column, a precedent for Roman imperial victory monuments.

design.description: The column is a Doric order structure made of Carrara marble, standing 29.6 m tall with a 10.1 m base.
Its shaft contains a spiral staircase of 190–200 steps, illuminated through narrow slits in the marble.
The column's frieze is a 112 m long spiral relief depicting scenes of the emperor's campaigns.

art.description: The relief shows the emperor's campaigns against Germanic and Sarmatian tribes, with dramatic scenes such as the miracle rain.
The symbolic language of the frieze emphasizes imperial dominance and authority, using clear but clumsy figures.
The depiction of the miracle rain scene illustrates divine intervention during the Marcomannic Wars.
